what_its_for: Prazosin is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension). It works by relaxing your blood vessels so your heart does not have to work as hard to pump blood. It may also be used off-label to reduce nightmares and sleep problems related to PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder).
how_to_take: Take prazosin by mouth exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food. Swallow the capsule whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time each day. Because this medicine can cause dizziness, especially with your first dose, your doctor may ask you to take your first dose at bedtime. Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel well.
dosing: Your doctor will usually start you on a low dose (1 mg, two to three times a day) and slowly increase it to find the dose that works best for you. The typical dose for high blood pressure ranges from 1 mg to 20 mg per day, split into two or three doses. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store prazosin at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused or expired medicine safely — ask your pharmacist about a drug take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking prazosin because it can increase dizziness and raise your risk of fainting. Be careful when standing up quickly from sitting or lying down, as this medicine can cause a sudden drop in blood pressure (dizziness or lightheadedness). Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid hot tubs, saunas, or prolonged standing in the heat, which can lower blood pressure further.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience: sudden severe dizziness or fainting, a fast or irregular heartbeat, chest pain, shortness of breath, swelling in your hands or feet, or if you feel like you might pass out. Also call your doctor if you develop a prolonged or painful erection (priapism) lasting more than 4 hours — this is a medical emergency. Let your doctor know if your blood pressure does not improve or gets worse.
when_it_works: Prazosin begins to lower blood pressure within a few hours of your first dose. However, it may take several weeks of regular use to get the full benefit for blood pressure control. For PTSD-related nightmares, some people notice improvement within the first one to two weeks, but it can take longer for others. Keep taking it as directed even if you feel fine.
special_populations: Older adults: You may be more sensitive to the blood pressure-lowering and dizziness effects of prazosin. Use extra caution when standing up to avoid falls. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before taking this medicine if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Children: Use in children should only be as directed by a pediatric specialist. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted.
